title: ASASSN-14ko UV peaks come later after the X-ray dip in broad flares, optical peaks keep a fixed 9.3-day lag, and shape-independent markers show that the period decrease stopped near 2021
abstract: Question: campaign studies found that the soft X-ray dip of the repeating nuclear transient ASASSN-14ko repeats at a constant 108.45-d period in 2020-2024 and stays 5.5 d before the UVW2 peak, so the period decrease stopped and the late flares are not a UV emission delay. But all flares in that lag test had narrow UV rises, the flares became broader after 2021, and the UVW2 peaks alone still showed a period decrease. Does the dip-to-peak time depend on flare shape, and which marker is independent of shape? Approach: we fitted one profile model (half-Gaussian rise of width s, exponential decline; MCMC) to every Swift UVW2 flare (2020-2024) and every ASAS-SN g/V flare (2014-2025), and fitted the peaks jointly with the published X-ray dip times on one clock plus a delay L0 + b (s - 2 d). Results: the UVW2 peak delay grows with the UV rise width, b = 0.60 d per d (95 percent 0.23-0.90; delta chi2 = 7.7 against a fixed lag), robust to the dip marker, clock form, priors and leaving out any flare (permutation p = 0.011); an X-ray-free check (UV minus optical peak) has the same sign but is not significant. The 5.5-d lag holds only for narrow flares: flare 33 (2024 July, s = 5.4 d) has its dip on the clock but its UV peak 11.4 d later. The ASAS-SN g peak has no shape term (b = 0.00, 95 percent -0.22 to 0.25) and follows the X-ray clock with a fixed 9.3-d lag and 0.67 d scatter. With the shape term the UVW2 peaks no longer show a period decrease. Shape-independent markers (X-ray dips, ASAS-SN and TESS peaks) reject a constant Pdot (delta AIC 11-12) and give a decrease with Pdot -0.0026 to -0.0029 up to cycle 23-24 (2021), then a constant period near 108.3 d; a later shorter period is only weakly favoured (delta AIC 2). Limitations: ten UV peaks, with flares 28, 29 and 33 giving most of the lever arm; the single-rise profile fits the two-stage 2022-2023 flares poorly; no new X-ray dips; our markers cannot separate an orbital change from a change of the fallback time.

display.caption: ASASSN-14ko flares aligned on the soft X-ray clock (P = 108.45 d). Left: four flares with narrow UV rises; right: four with broad UV rises. Rows: Swift XRT 0.3-2 keV, UVW2 and ASAS-SN g. The X-ray drop stays at day 0; the UV peak comes later in broad flares, the g peak does not.

Peak minus the X-ray clock against the rise width. UVW2 peaks have a delay of 0.60 d per day of rise width; ASAS-SN g peaks have none. Right: UVW2 peak minus the X-ray dip of the same flare; the 5.5-d lag holds only for narrow flares.

O-C of shape-independent markers (X-ray dips, our ASAS-SN g/V peaks, TESS peaks, published peaks) against 108.45 d, with constant-Pdot, one-break and two-break clocks. The period decrease stops near cycle 23-24 (2021).

citations.reason: We use its XRT counts and box-ingress samples. Its constant 5.5-d dip-to-UV lag holds only for narrow-rise flares (flare 33 has 11.4 d), but its constant-period X-ray clock agrees with our shape-independent optical peaks.

We use its 30 and 50 percent X-ray dip times as the X-ray clock. Its constant lead on the UV peak was tested only on narrow flares; the deep-suppression clock itself agrees with the optical peaks to 0.67 d.
Its finding that the UVW2 peaks show a period decrease in 2020-2023 (no stall) comes from the broad UV flares; with the shape term the UV peaks agree with the X-ray clock.
Its broader optical rises after 2021 motivated this test; our homogeneous fits agree that optical peak times do not depend on the rise width.
We use its Swift UVOT UVW2 per-visit photometry.
We use its archived ASAS-SN Sky Patrol light curve, TESS peak fits and published-peak table; our homogeneous peaks confirm a constant period near 108 d after 2021.
Random period kicks of about 0.6 d per orbit still describe the 2014-2025 record, but in 2020-2024 the optical peaks scatter by only 0.67 d about one linear clock.
Part of the timing noise it found can come from mixing UV and optical markers whose lag depends on flare shape.
A shape-dependent UV emission delay exists (up to about 6 d), but the optical peak and the X-ray dip do not show it, so it cannot replace the period change.
Later SPHEREx timing (cycle 37) that our markers do not cover; input listed for completeness.
Payne et al. (2022) ephemeris (Pdot = -0.0026) and published peak times; our early-era Pdot agrees, the later decrease stops.
